analysis.one_liner: Requires far more paid political consultants and advisers to register and disclose as lobbyists.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make thousands of behind-the-scenes political advisers register as lobbyists, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since the day it was introduced, backed by 6 House Democrats and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would close two well-known gaps in the federal lobbying disclosure law. First, it would treat paid "strategic counselors" — people who coach, plan, and advise on lobbying behind the scenes without ever making the contact themselves — as lobbyists who must register and disclose their clients. Second, it would cut the time threshold for forced registration in half, from 20% of a person's work time to 10%, so many more professional influencers would have to file public disclosure reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a clearer public record of who is paid to influence Congress and the executive branch: right now, a whole tier of consultants, former officials, and advisers can shape legislation for paying clients without ever appearing in the public lobbying database. Journalists, watchdog groups, and the public would be able to see those relationships. Firms that already play by the disclosure rules would also face slightly fairer competition against rivals who currently dodge registration.

how_it_helps.text: Closes the 'strategic counselor' loophole: anyone paid to provide legislative, political, or strategic counseling in support of a lobbying contact — and who knows the contact was made — would be treated as having made that contact themselves, and would have to register and disclose under the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
Cuts the registration time threshold in half, from 20% to 10% of a person's paid work time, so professionals who spend a smaller share of their time on lobbying would no longer escape registration.
Expands what counts as a 'lobbying activity' to include the preparation, planning, counseling, and research that support lobbying contacts, rather than only the contacts themselves.
Takes effect immediately upon enactment for all lobbying contacts made after that date, so the new disclosure requirements would apply without a phase-in delay.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms, law firms, and consultancies that sell political strategy and access would bear the cost: more of their staff and outside advisers would have to register, file quarterly disclosure reports naming their clients, and operate under the restrictions that come with registered-lobbyist status. Some firms that currently bill clients for 'advisory' work kept off the public ledger would lose that discretion, and clients would have their paid influence made public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lobbying firms and paid political advisers

drawbacks.text: The language is broad: phrases like 'counseling in support of' and 'substantially influence' could sweep in routine policy advice from lawyers, public-relations firms, and consultants who never intended to lobby, creating compliance uncertainty and probably litigation over who counts.

Cutting the registration threshold to 10% of work time would pull in people with only incidental lobbying roles, adding paperwork for small consultancies, nonprofits, and state or local groups whose federal work is minor — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.
The bill takes effect the day it is signed, with no phase-in, so firms would need to reclassify staff and file disclosures almost immediately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure gains are real: the biggest known gap in the Lobbying Disclosure Act is the 'strategic adviser' tier of consultants who shape lobbying without ever making the call, and this bill directly targets that gap while also halving the time threshold. The cost is a heavier and somewhat fuzzy compliance burden, and the broad drafting could over-capture ordinary advice. A careful version would phase in the 10% threshold and define counseling more precisely. On balance, more public disclosure of paid influence is worth the compliance cost, but the bill as drafted is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on the same day in January 2026, and it has not moved since — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the bill on January 22, 2026, with three original cosponsors: Reps. Nikema Williams of Georgia, Kevin Mullin, and Lateefah Simon.
The same day, the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which has jurisdiction over lobbying and disclosure law.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been taken on it since the referral — no committee markup, no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and paid strategic advisers are better off so far: as long as the bill sits untouched in committee, their behind-the-scenes work for paying clients stays off the public disclosure books. Members who avoid casting a recorded vote on lobbying disclosure also benefit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbying firms whose work stays undisclosed

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been taken, but all six members of Congress attached to the bill — the sponsor and five cosponsors — are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: These firms profit from a system where high-priced 'strategic counselors' can influence policy without ever registering or naming clients. The bill would force that work onto the public disclosure books and double the pool of staff who must register.

industries.industry: Law and consulting firms selling political strategy
industries.note: Lawyers and consultancies that bill clients for 'advisory' work kept off the lobbying ledger would have to register those relationships and disclose them quarterly, exposing client lists they currently keep private.

industries.industry: Trade associations and corporate government-affairs offices
industries.note: More of their in-house staff and outside advisers would cross the registration threshold and their paid influence campaigns would become public, though core in-house lobbying was already disclosable.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. With one sponsor, five cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action in months, the most likely path is the most common one: it sits in the Judiciary Committee until the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and dies without a vote. Ethics and lobbying-disclosure bills rarely get floor time without a scandal or bipartisan leadership backing, neither of which is present here.
